description: Elinor Ostrom's conceptual distinction between a common-pool resource (a good type), a common property regime (a property regime) and open access. Captures what counts as a commons in her terminology and what does not.

words.name: good type
words.description: Classification of goods along subtractability of use and difficulty of exclusion (Ostrom & Ostrom 1977 typology).

words.name: common-pool resource
words.description: Resource system with high subtractability of use and high cost of exclusion; a property of the good, not of its ownership.

words.name: private good
words.description: High subtractability, low exclusion cost.

words.name: public good
words.description: Low subtractability, high exclusion cost.

words.name: club good
words.description: Low subtractability, low exclusion cost; also called toll good.

words.name: subtractability
words.description: Degree to which one user's consumption reduces what remains available to others; defining criterion of a common-pool resource.

words.name: exclusion cost
words.description: Cost of preventing non-authorized persons from using the resource; defining criterion of a common-pool resource.

words.name: resource system
words.description: The stock that generates a flow, e.g. a fishery, an aquifer, an alpine pasture.

words.name: resource unit
words.description: What appropriators withdraw from the system, e.g. a caught fish; usually becomes private property upon withdrawal even under a common property regime.

words.name: property regime
words.description: Institutional arrangement assigning bundles of rights over a resource; independent of the good type.

words.name: common property regime
words.description: Property regime in which a defined group of co-owners holds rights and enforces rules; not the absence of property.

words.name: open access
words.description: Absence of enforced rights and of a defined user group; res nullius. Explicitly not a commons in Ostrom's terminology.

words.name: state property
words.description: Property regime with government as rights holder; nationalization of commons has repeatedly converted working common property regimes into de facto open access.

words.name: private property
words.description: Property regime with individual rights holders including alienation.

words.name: commons
words.description: A common-pool resource governed under a common property regime; requires both the good type and the institution.

words.name: knowledge commons
words.description: Shared knowledge or information resource; low subtractability, so the governance problem is provision and enclosure rather than overuse.

words.name: bundle of rights
words.description: Set of distinguishable rights over a resource; ownership is not binary.

words.name: access right
words.description: Right to enter a defined physical property.

words.name: withdrawal right
words.description: Right to obtain resource units.

words.name: management right
words.description: Right to regulate internal use patterns and transform the resource.

words.name: exclusion right
words.description: Right to determine who holds access and withdrawal rights.

words.name: alienation right
words.description: Right to sell or lease management and exclusion rights.

words.name: rights holder
words.description: Position defined by which subset of the bundle of rights is held.

words.name: authorized user
words.description: Holds access and withdrawal rights only.

words.name: claimant
words.description: Holds access, withdrawal and management rights.

words.name: proprietor
words.description: Holds access, withdrawal, management and exclusion rights, but not alienation.

words.name: owner
words.description: Holds the full bundle including alienation.

words.name: design principle
words.description: Regularity found in long-enduring self-governed common-pool resource institutions; diagnostic, not a recipe.

words.name: clearly defined boundaries
words.description: First design principle: both the resource and the set of authorized users must be defined; its absence marks open access rather than a commons.

words.name: tragedy of the commons
words.description: Hardin's 1968 model of inevitable degradation; it assumes open access, which is why Ostrom regarded the label as a misnomer.

words.name: Toerbel
words.description: Village in Valais, Switzerland; alpine meadows, forests, irrigation channels and paths held under a common property regime alongside private arable plots. Ostrom's paradigmatic long-enduring case.

words.name: count
words.description: Number of items.

words.name: year
words.description: Calendar year.

words.name: measured value
words.description: Value taken from a cited source.

words.name: assumed value
words.description: Value estimated in this dataset, to be given a confidence.

triples.name: subtractability criterion
triples.description: High subtractability is one of the two defining criteria.

triples.name: exclusion criterion
triples.description: High exclusion cost is the second defining criterion.

triples.name: open access as regime
triples.description: Listed as a regime for completeness; it is the null case, with no enforced rights.

triples.name: tragedy assumes open access
triples.description: The model describes open access; applying it to common property regimes is the confusion Ostrom set out to correct.

sources.name: ostrom-1990
sources.description: Ostrom, E. (1990). Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. Cambridge University Press.

sources.name: ostrom-et-al-1999
sources.description: Ostrom, E., Burger, J., Field, C. B., Norgaard, R. B., Policansky, D. (1999). Revisiting the Commons: Local Lessons, Global Challenges. Science 284(5412), 278-282. DOI 10.1126/science.284.5412.278

sources.name: schlager-ostrom-1992
sources.description: Schlager, E., Ostrom, E. (1992). Property-Rights Regimes and Natural Resources: A Conceptual Analysis. Land Economics 68(3), 249-262. DOI 10.2307/3146375

sources.description: Ostrom, E. (2010). Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems. American Economic Review 100(3), 641-672.

sources.description: Hardin, G. (1968). The Tragedy of the Commons. Science 162(3859), 1243-1248. DOI not verified in this session.
